keyVerseText: O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall. digged: or, houghed oxen
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun רָצוֹן (râtsôwn) derives from the root רָצָה (râtsâh), which conveys the idea of being pleased with or accepting something favorably. This root sense emphasizes an inward delight or approval, suggesting more than mere acceptance—it implies a heartfelt goodwill or voluntary desire. Thus, רָצוֹן carries the nuance of what is pleasing or agreeable to the will, highlighting a personal or divine favor rather than a neutral state.
usageInScripture: With 56 occurrences, רָצוֹן consistently appears in contexts expressing favor, goodwill, and acceptance, both from God and humans. Its top translations such as 'favour,' 'according to his will,' and 'thy will' reveal a strong association with divine pleasure and human desire aligned with God’s purposes. The word also appears in sacrificial contexts, indicating acceptance before the Lord, which underscores its theological depth as reflecting relational harmony and voluntary consent.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding רָצוֹן enriches our grasp of God's relational nature—He is not a distant deity but one who delights in His people and their obedience. The word reveals that God's acceptance is not merely legal but rooted in His goodwill and pleasure, which invites believers into a gracious fellowship. For the Christian faith, this underscores the importance of aligning our wills with God's, seeking to live in a way that is not only obedient but pleasing to Him. It also points to Christ’s role as the ultimate sacrifice that finds divine favor, reconciling us to God’s will and pleasure.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 49:6 warns against joining in the secret assemblies of those who act in anger and self-will, highlighting the destructive nature of following one’s own pleasure apart from God’s favor. The use of רָצוֹן here in the phrase 'in their selfwill they digged down a wall' contrasts human self-centered desire with the divine will. It serves as a caution that true honor and acceptance come not from pursuing personal desires but from submitting to God’s righteous will.
